evidence_quotes.quote: In 2018, anonymous semi-structured interviews were organized; the questionnaire was comprised of 17 questions about residents’ perceptions, choices, practices, and access to resources such as fresh food, drinking water, and electricity (Table 1).

Thus, we deﬁned a set of 12 indicators that reﬂect residents’ perceptions of WEF safety (Table 2). Additionally, for each indicator, a threshold was deﬁned, based on existing public policies and programs in Brazilian legislation or, if no thresholds were established for the indicator, we considered international standards as a reference.

The sampling method used was the conglomerate. We split the neighborhood into three sectors, randomly selecting the blocks by drawing one at a time (Figure 2). If no respondent was available, the team picked the next household instead.

Despite this, 14 of the interviewees report daily rationing of public water supply services. As a way to save water, 13 residents reported practices such as reusing greywater and rainwater harvesting (Figure 4).

In Itinga, there is no public sewage treatment, depending exclusively on individual solutions. 17 of the interviewees afﬁrmed using a septic tank and 13 respondents consider sewage treatment inadequate.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household water supply and sanitation service access in Itinga (Angra dos Reis, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil), surveying residents on public water connection, daily rationing/intermittency, perceived water quality, and household sewage disposal/septic tanks.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing water or sanitation access (such as eligibility screening, tenure or documentation rules, tariffs/cost recovery, administrative burden, enforcement, discretion, or utility regulatory structure) is examined; a brief parenthetical personal-communication remark notes that 80 families lacked regular electricity in 2016 due to living in prohibited areas, which concerns electricity rather than water/sanitation and is not empirically analyzed. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, although the study references national and municipal policy goals (e.g., National Basic Sanitation Plan and UN 2030 Agenda targets) to set benchmark thresholds for a 12-indicator Water-Energy-Food (WEF) nexus dashboard and situates the site within macro urbanization/irregular-occupation background, it does not empirically analyze any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor in relation to water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a 2018 semi-structured household survey of 22 randomly sampled households across three sectors in Itinga, paired with indicator mapping to official Brazilian datasets.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive household outcomes on public water supply connection (21 of 22 interviewees), daily water rationing (14 of 22), water supply interruptions up to three days, perceived water quality, and absence of public sewage network / reliance on septic tanks (17 of 22) and perceived inadequacy of sewage treatment (13 of 22).
criterion_notes.c5: Population (adult residents in 22 surveyed households in Itinga, Angra dos Reis), descriptive water/sanitation outcomes, and cross-sectional case-study survey design are identifiable, but no legal, administrative, or governance exposure variable is empirically examined (descriptive WEF indicator-framework construction in a single neglected neighborhood).

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods (quali-quantitative) household survey and indicator-development case study
population_and_sample: Adult residents (over 18 years old) in Itinga neighborhood, Angra dos Reis municipality, Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil; sample of 22 households (unit of analysis: household/interviewee)
exposure: not reported (descriptive Water-Energy-Food nexus indicator framework development in a peri-urban neglected neighborhood; no legal, administrative, or governance exposure analyzed)
outcome: Household perceptions and self-reported status of water supply connection, daily rationing and supply interruptions, drinking water quality, and septic tank / sewage disposal adequacy (alongside electricity and food consumption indicators)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the paper empirically describes household water supply, rationing, water quality perceptions, and sewage/septic conditions among 22 households in Itinga, Brazil, its purpose and analysis consist of constructing a participatory 12-indicator Water-Energy-Food (WEF) nexus assessment framework linked to official datasets and policy target thresholds. It does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism governing water or sanitation service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, nor does it empirically analyze any broader governance or institutional exposure under the plain wording of Criterion 2.
